cards.title: Title
cues: Gabriel Mamane · Night Signal
How accurately can a cheap wearable measure blood oxygen?
Can software flag oxygen drops?
NOT a test for sleep apnea
cards.script: Good morning. My name is Gabriel Mamane. My project, Night Signal, asks how accurately a low-cost wearable can measure blood oxygen and heart rate, and whether software can flag drops in oxygen. It is not a test for sleep apnea.

cards.title: Purpose & hypothesis
cues: Q: does the wearable agree with a Health Canada-authorized fingertip oximeter? (SpO₂ + heart rate)
Can it flag desaturations: ≥ 3 points for ≥ 10 s?
H: within ±3 points (95% limits of agreement)
Why: both use red + infrared light
Change: device + condition → Measure: difference, events, % valid
cards.next: Some background on how this works.
cards.script: My question is how closely my wearable's oxygen and heart-rate readings agree with a Health Canada-authorized fingertip oximeter, and whether software can reliably flag oxygen desaturation events. My hypothesis is that, when it is worn properly and only good-quality readings are used, it will agree within about three percentage points, because both devices measure how blood absorbs red and infrared light. What I change is the measuring device and the test condition; what I measure is the difference between the two devices, the events flagged, and how much of the signal is valid.

cards.title: Scientific background
cues: Red 660 nm + infrared 880 nm → SpO₂
Desaturation = short drop; sleep studies use ≥ 3% plus other signals
Apnea diagnosis = sleep study: airflow, breathing effort, sleep
Not every drop is an apnea; not every apnea causes a drop
So: accuracy + oxygen dips, NOT diagnosis
cards.next: Here is the device I designed.
cards.script: A pulse oximeter shines red and infrared light through the fingertip; oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood absorb them differently, which gives the oxygen saturation, SpO2. A desaturation is a short drop in SpO2, and sleep studies count drops of three percent or more, but only together with other signals. Sleep apnea is diagnosed with a sleep study that measures airflow, breathing effort and sleep itself. My device measures only oxygen and heart rate, so it cannot tell an apnea from other causes of a dip, and it would miss apneas that cause little or no drop. That is why my project is about measurement accuracy and oxygen dips, not about diagnosing sleep apnea.

cards.script: This is the design. The first prototype keeps things simple: an ESP32 board in a running armband, a MAX30102 sensor in a velcro finger cuff, and a USB cable for power, with every wire plugged in. It reads oxygen and heart rate once per second. The 3D model shows a possible later version in a sealed case. The prototype has not been built yet; the parts list and build guide are ready.

cues: Sensor → ESP32 → Bluetooth / USB → app + analysis

cards.script: The finger sensor's light readings go to the ESP32, which calculates oxygen and pulse once per second and sends each reading over Bluetooth or USB to my app and analysis code. Every session will start with a device check that must say READY. So far I have tested this check only on a simulated device, where it also correctly reported a broken sensor; it still has to be tested on the real hardware.

Every reading must pass the quality checks

cards.next: The app shows all of this.
cards.script: This is my planned protocol. Nothing will be tested on anyone, including me, until my teacher accepts this revised proposal, the ethics committee approves, and consent is signed. The main test is accuracy: seated at rest, I wear my device on one finger and the reference oximeter on the other hand, and I record both oxygen and heart rate every two minutes for thirty minutes, over several sessions. Every reading must pass signal-quality checks. If approved, overnight recordings will measure signal quality and desaturation events, but those events cannot be verified because the reference oximeter does not record overnight. An optional breath-hold test, only if approved, would check whether short, awake dips are flagged; it does not test sleep apnea.

cards.script: This is my companion app. The Night tab shows the oxygen chart, the desaturation events it flagged, the event rate per hour of valid recording and how much of the signal was valid. The Live tab connects to the wearable and runs the device checks. Everything you see so far is clearly labelled demonstration data.

The table shows each measure, how it is calculated, and a demonstration value from simulated data, which only proves that my analysis code runs; they are not findings. The event rate is the number of desaturation events divided by the hours of valid signal, not hours in bed, and it is not an apnea-hypopnea index. cards.title: Demonstration charts
cues: Left: oxygen line, red bands = flagged dips (simulated)
Right: Bland–Altman; each dot = one pair of readings

cards.script: These two charts show how the results will be presented, using simulated data. On the left, the oxygen line with each flagged desaturation event as a red band. On the right, a Bland-Altman chart, the standard way to compare two measuring devices: each dot is a pair of readings, and the dashed lines show the range that ninety-five percent of differences fall in. With real data, that range is what tests my hypothesis.

cards.title: Signal quality
cues: 4 checks: finger on · sensor-valid · 70–100% · no movement within 5 s
Rate = flagged events ÷ hours of valid signal
Not per hour of sleep: the device cannot measure sleep
Every report states the % of valid signal
cards.next: How I will interpret the results.
cards.script: Only good readings count. A reading is used only if a finger is on the sensor, the sensor marks it valid, it is in a believable range, and there was no sudden movement within five seconds. The event rate is the number of flagged events divided by the hours of valid signal. It is not per hour of sleep, because my device cannot measure sleep, and every report states how much of the signal was valid.

cards.title: Analysis: interpretation
cues: Supported if 95% of differences are within ±3 points (at rest)
The reference itself is typically about ±2 points
Flagged event = oxygen dip, not apnea; overnight unverified
Breath-holds: only awake, induced dips
Against: wide limits, bias, low % valid, missed dips
cards.script: This is how I will interpret the results. If ninety-five percent of the oxygen differences fall within three points of the reference at rest, my hypothesis is supported for those conditions, keeping in mind that the reference is itself typically accurate to about two points. A flagged event means an oxygen dip, not an apnea, and overnight events cannot be checked because the reference does not record overnight. The breath-hold test, if approved, shows only whether awake dips are flagged. Wider limits, a consistent bias, too little valid signal, or missed dips would count against my hypothesis.

cards.title: Sources of error
cues: Measurement: movement, pressure, cold hands, light
Skin tone can bias oximeters (Sjoding et al., 2020)
Method: no airflow / effort / sleep → cannot identify apnea
Awake ≠ asleep; breath-hold ≠ apnea; one participant
Battery 4–5 h = estimate → USB power for v1
cards.script: Sources of error in measurement: movement, finger pressure, cold hands and room light can distort the light signal; research has shown pulse oximeters can be less accurate on darker skin; and the reference is typically accurate to only about two points. In the method: my device measures only oxygen and heart rate, so it cannot identify apnea; sitting awake is not the same as sleep, and a breath-hold is not an apnea; there is only one participant; and overnight events cannot be verified. I also estimated that a small battery would last only four to five hours, which is why the first prototype is planned to use USB power; I still have to measure that.

Thank you. Questions?
cards.script: I do not have a conclusion yet, because no real data has been collected. After the accuracy sessions, this project will show how closely the wearable agrees with a reference oximeter at rest, how much of a recording gives a valid signal, and, if approved, whether flagged dips match logged ones. It cannot show whether anyone has sleep apnea. Thank you; I am happy to take questions.

qa: Can your device detect sleep apnea?
No. It measures only oxygen and heart rate. Diagnosing sleep apnea needs a sleep study that also measures airflow, breathing effort and sleep. My software flags oxygen dips only.

It is a realistic target for a low-cost sensor: a little wider than the reference oximeter's own typical ±2 points. The international standard for pulse oximeters (ISO 80601-2-61) allows a root-mean-square error of up to 4 points.

Each dot is one pair of readings: the difference between the devices against their average. The bias is the average difference, and the 95% limits of agreement show where 95% of differences fall. It is the standard way to compare two measuring methods (Bland & Altman, 1986).
Two devices can rise and fall together but still disagree, for example if one always reads 3 points high. Agreement has to be measured from the differences.
How do you know a reading is good?
Four checks: a finger is on the sensor, the sensor marks the reading valid, SpO₂ is between 70 and 100%, and there was no sudden movement within 5 seconds. Each report states the % of valid signal.
Why events per hour of VALID signal?
If the sensor loses the signal, dividing by time in bed would make the rate look lower than it is. It is also not an apnea–hypopnea index (AHI).
Is the testing safe and approved?

Nothing is tested on anyone, including me, until Ms. Ireland accepts the revised proposal, ethics approval is issued and consent is signed. Breath-holds are optional, 20 s at most, seated and supervised, and stop at any discomfort or below 90% on the reference.
Yes. Research has found that pulse oximeters can overestimate oxygen in people with darker skin (Sjoding et al., 2020). With one participant I cannot test this; it is a limitation.
Build the prototype, run the accuracy sessions, and, with approval, test more participants and compare against a lab-grade reference.
